name: Alpheus (father of James son of Alpheus)
title: Father of the Apostle James the Less
summary: Alpheus is a New Testament figure known exclusively as the father of the apostle James – one of the twelve, often referred to as "James the younger" or "son of Alpheus," in distinction from James the son of Zebedee. His name appears in all four lists of apostles in the New Testament, in the Synoptic Gospels and in Acts, yet he never acts as an independent character in any of the narratives. Despite this anonymity, the name Alpheus raises several interesting questions. A widespread church tradition identifies his wife with Mary mentioned at the cross in Mark 15:40 as mother of "James the younger and Joses." It has also been discussed whether he might be identical to Cleopas, mentioned in John 19:25, or with the Alpheus who is called father of the tax collector Levi in Mark 2:14. However, both these connections remain disputed and unconfirmed based solely on the New Testament texts.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned as James' father in the lists of apostles
keyEvents.description: Alpheus is mentioned as the father of the Apostle James in the lists of Jesus' twelve disciples. His son was called by Jesus to be among the twelve apostles. The patronymic 'son of Alpheus' appears in all four apostle lists in the New Testament.

keyEvents.title: Possible connection to Mary at the cross
keyEvents.description: At Jesus' crucifixion, Mary, the mother of James the Less and Joses, is mentioned among the women who were present. If this James is identical with the Apostle James son of Alpheus, then this Mary was Alpheus' wife. She is also mentioned among the women who came to the tomb on Easter morning.

keyEvents.title: Possible connection to Levi/Matthew's father
keyEvents.description: In Mark 2:14, the tax collector Levi is called 'son of Alpheus'. It is debated among scholars whether this Alpheus is the same as the father of the Apostle James. If they are identical, James and Levi (traditionally identified with Matthew) would have been brothers, but this is not explicitly confirmed in any New Testament text.

versions.summary: Alpheus is a figure in the New Testament known exclusively through his patronymic – as father of the apostle James, often called "James the younger" or "James son of Alpheus." This designation serves to distinguish him from the other apostle named James, son of Zebedee. The name Alpheus appears in all four lists of apostles in the New Testament: in the Synoptic Gospels and in Acts. Although he never appears as an independent actor in the narratives, his name has given rise to several interesting questions. A widespread tradition identifies his wife with Mary, mother of "James the younger and Joses," who is mentioned at the cross in Mark 15:40. It has also been discussed whether he might be identical with Cleopas (John 19:25) or with the Alpheus named as father of the tax collector Levi in Mark 2:14, but both connections remain uncertain.

footnotes.text: The Greek name Ἁλφαῖος (Halphaios) is thought to derive from the Aramaic חַלְפַּי (Halfai), which may mean "replacement" or "successor". Some scholars have suggested a link to Κλωπᾶς (Klopas) in John 19:25, but the etymological differences between the names make this identification highly uncertain.

In Mark 15:40, "Mary, the mother of James the younger and Joses" is mentioned among the women at the crucifixion. This James is traditionally identified as the son of the apostle James son of Alphaeus, making this Mary the wife of Alphaeus. However, this identification is not explicitly confirmed in the text.

Two individuals named Alphaeus are mentioned in the New Testament: the father of the apostle James and the father of the tax collector Levi (Mark 2:14). If these refer to the same person, James and Levi (possibly identified with Matthew) would have been brothers—but no New Testament text directly confirms this, and many scholars regard them as two different individuals.

Alphaeus is among the most anonymous figures in the New Testament. He never appears as an independent actor but occurs exclusively as a patronym for his son James. Nor did any independent tradition about him develop in early church history.

In ancient Jewish culture, the patronymic—the father's name—was a central part of personal identification. The fact that James is consistently called "son of Alphaeus" in all apostle lists suggests this was necessary to distinguish him from the far more prominent apostle James, son of Zebedee.

Church tradition has attempted to harmonize the various references to Alphaeus in the New Testament. Jerome (c. 347–420) argued that Alphaeus, Cleopas, and Klopas all referred to the same person, but this view has received limited support in modern scholarship due to a lack of textual and etymological evidence.
